overview: Pachycephalosaurus wyomingensis ("thick-headed lizard") was the largest pachycephalosaur — a dome-headed ornithischian from the Hell Creek Formation of the latest Cretaceous North America (~68–66 Ma) reaching about five metres. Its skull roof is a dome of solid bone up to 25 cm thick, reinforced internally by struts and surrounded by a ring of bony knobs and spikes. Whether this dome was used for head-butting combat or lateral flank-pushing is actively debated.

Pachycephalosaurus is relatively rare in the Hell Creek Formation and known mainly from skulls — the extremely dense dome bone preserves well while the rest of the skeleton, being more fragile, rarely survives. It represents the culmination of the pachycephalosaur lineage that originated in the early Late Cretaceous and diversified across North America and Asia.

fossilSites.name: Hell Creek Formation
fossilSites.note: Latest Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) beds with Pachycephalosaurus dome skulls — often found in isolation as the most preservable element.

articles.title: Discovery and the dome
articles.body: Named by Brown and Schlaikjer in 1943 from Hell Creek material. The skull dome is the most distinctive feature — a solid mass of cancellous and compact bone up to 25 cm thick. The dome grows through ontogeny: juveniles and sub-adults have thinner, flatter domes that become increasingly domed with age. Stygimoloch and Dracorex — previously named as separate genera — are now widely considered juvenile and sub-adult Pachycephalosaurus.

articles.title: Head-butting debate
articles.body: The head-butting hypothesis — where rival males charged each other dome-to-dome like bighorn sheep — has been the default interpretation since the 1970s. However, finite element analysis shows the dome transmits stress poorly in a direct head-to-head collision. Flank-pushing (butting the flanks of rivals, as in musk oxen) is an alternative. The dome shape, angular position of the skull relative to the vertebral column, and presence of skull pathologies interpreted as impact injuries all inform this debate.

articles.title: Pachycephalosaur evolutionary significance
articles.body: Pachycephalosauria is the sister group of Ceratopsia within Marginocephalia — a relationship supported by shared thickening of the skull roof (though taken to very different extremes in each group). Both groups are restricted to the Cretaceous and represent the last major ornithischian diversification. Pachycephalosaurus was one of the last surviving pachycephalosaurs before the K-Pg extinction.

facts: Histology and morphology support interpreting Dracorex as a juvenile and Stygimoloch as a younger stage or close taxon, though details remain debated.
The thick dome is directly preserved, but combat style is inferred rather than observed.
Body size is less secure than skull anatomy because associated skeletons are rare.

presentation.heroLead: The largest of the dome-headed dinosaurs, known almost entirely from thick skull roofs whose changing shape through growth has redrawn the family tree of its relatives.

animalParagraphs: Pachycephalosaurus was a two-legged ornithischian from the final two million years of the Cretaceous, living alongside Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops and Edmontosaurus on the floodplains of western North America. It is the largest known pachycephalosaur, with skulls approaching 60 centimetres in length; body length estimates of around four and a half metres rest on scaling the skull against smaller relatives.

Its defining feature is a solid dome of bone on the skull roof, up to about 25 centimetres thick, ringed by bony knobs and, at the back of the skull, short spikes. Small, leaf-shaped cheek teeth suggest a diet of soft plants, though the front of the jaw carried more pointed teeth and an omnivorous diet has been proposed.

Growth studies of dozens of skull roofs suggest the dome only formed late in life. Younger animals had flat skulls and long spikes, and the animals once named Dracorex and Stygimoloch are now widely, though not universally, regarded as juvenile and subadult Pachycephalosaurus.
animalHighlights: A thickened skull dome up to about 25 cm deep, surrounded by knobs and short spikes on the squamosal bones.
Skull roofs from many individuals record a growth series from flat-headed juveniles to fully domed adults.
Small, serrated cheek teeth and pointed front teeth leave the exact diet open; postcranial bones are rarely preserved.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Leaf-shaped cheek teeth support a plant diet; heterodont front teeth have prompted suggestions of omnivory. No gut contents are known.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Pachycephalosaur postcrania from better-known genera such as Stegoceras and Homalocephale are bipedal; Pachycephalosaurus itself has little limb material.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: No complete skeleton exists. Length and mass estimates scale skull size against smaller pachycephalosaurs and carry wide error.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Dome, knobs and spikes are directly preserved; body shape, skin and colour follow other pachycephalosaurs.

presentation.classificationSummary: Pachycephalosaurus gives its name to Pachycephalosauria and Pachycephalosauridae, the dome-headed ornithischians allied to the horned dinosaurs within Marginocephalia. Whether Dracorex and Stygimoloch are growth stages of Pachycephalosaurus or distinct genera remains the main taxonomic question.

A flat-skulled form now usually read as a juvenile stage of Pachycephalosaurus.
A smaller, older pachycephalosaur known from a partial skeleton, the main reference for body form.

questions.title: What was the dome for?
questions.copy: Head-to-head or flank butting is inferred from dome shape, neck anatomy and healed skull lesions found on many domes, but no behaviour was ever observed and display remains a live alternative.

questions.title: Are Dracorex and Stygimoloch the same animal?
questions.copy: Bone histology and skull shape support a single growth series, yet some workers still treat Stygimoloch as distinct. The evidence is skull-only and sample sizes are small.

questions.title: What did the rest of the body look like?
questions.copy: Nearly all fossils are skull roofs. Limb, hip and tail anatomy are reconstructed from smaller relatives, so size estimates could shift if an associated skeleton is fully described.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
specimens.note: A partial skull roof from the Lance Formation of Niobrara County, Wyoming, first described by Gilmore in 1931 as Troodon wyomingensis and made the type of Pachycephalosaurus by Brown and Schlaikjer in 1943.

specimens.name: Referred skull
specimens.note: A nearly complete skull collected near Ekalaka, Carter County, Montana, in 1940; the holotype of the synonymised species P. grangeri and the most mature skull in published growth series.

specimens.name: Growth-series skulls and domes
specimens.institution: Museum of the Rockies, UCMP and other collections
specimens.note: Dozens of isolated domes and partial skulls across growth stages, including the specimens named Dracorex and Stygimoloch, which many workers now assign to Pachycephalosaurus.

panel.headline: Many skull roofs, a few good skulls, and almost no skeleton.
panel.standfirst: Pachycephalosaurus is documented by dozens of thick domes and partial skulls from the Lance and Hell Creek formations, spanning juveniles to old adults. Associated bones from the rest of the body are rare, so the animal below the head is largely reconstructed from smaller relatives.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: The skull is known from many individuals at several growth stages, but the vertebral column, girdles and limbs are represented only by sparse, mostly undescribed material.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Numerous frontoparietal domes and skull roofs, several nearly complete skulls with jaws and teeth, and a small amount of associated postcranial material from one partial skeleton.
knownRemains.note: Because most specimens are isolated domes, growth and pathology are well studied while body proportions, limb anatomy and mass remain poorly constrained.

media.title: Holotype skull roof USNM 12031
media.alt: Photograph of the Pachycephalosaurus wyomingensis holotype skull roof, USNM 12031, at the Smithsonian
media.caption: The name-bearing skull roof from the Lance Formation of Wyoming, showing the thickened dome and knobbed rim. The rest of the skull and the skeleton are not preserved in this specimen.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many domes and skull roofs; several near-complete skulls with braincase, snout and dentition, plus juvenile and subadult skulls.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Little described material; a partial skeleton nicknamed Sandy preserves some vertebrae and ribs but awaits full publication.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Sparse. Limb and hip anatomy are inferred from Stegoceras, Homalocephale and other pachycephalosaurs.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Healed lesions on many domes and bone histology across growth stages; no skin, colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: USNM 12031 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull roof collected from the Lance Formation of Wyoming. Gilmore described it in 1931 as a species of Troodon; Brown and Schlaikjer recognised it as a distinct dome-headed genus in 1943.
specimenCards.meta: Niobrara County, Wyoming · Lance Formation · Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

specimenCards.title: AMNH 1696 · referred skull
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete skull from Carter County, Montana, originally named Pachycephalosaurus grangeri. It anchors the adult end of the published growth series and shows the fully developed dome and reduced spikes.
specimenCards.meta: Ekalaka, Montana · Hell Creek Formation · American Museum of Natural History

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Thick domed skull roofs, knobbed and spiked skull margins, small heterodont teeth, skull lesions and a growth series from flat-headed juveniles to domed adults.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A bipedal marginocephalian whose dome grew late in life and was probably used in intraspecific combat or display; Dracorex and Stygimoloch as its younger growth stages.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Body proportions, adult mass, limb anatomy, diet in detail, how the dome was actually used, and whether every Hell Creek pachycephalosaur belongs to one species.
